claims.text: The target material is an FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating on conventional metals.
The overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings is governed by dynamic microstructural evolution.
Formation and stability of oxide layers govern the high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Redistribution of alloying elements governs the high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Oxide-layer evolution and alloying-element redistribution can be observed in real time using in-situ TEM or SEM during high-temperature wear tests.
Applying in-situ TEM or SEM is the proposed intervention relative to prior room-temperature or limited-thermal-regime studies.
Real-time observation of microstructural changes will improve understanding of the mechanism governing wear resistance.
The proposed hypothesis applies from 500°C to 1000°C.
The proposed hypothesis applies under loads from 10 N to 100 N.
A lack of correlation between microstructural evolution and wear resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve predicted improvements in wear resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome is improved mechanistic understanding rather than improved wear resistance, but the falsification rule refers to failure to obtain predicted improvements in wear resistance. No such directional wear improvement is actually predicted.

The stated intervention is observational application of in-situ TEM or SEM, whereas the falsification experiment additionally invokes controlled oxide-layer formation and alloying-element redistribution as material interventions without specifying how they are produced.
